paragraphs: The paper studies an eigenvalue problem with an added sparsity requirement: the solution must use only a limited set of coordinates. This connects eigenvalue calculations to applications such as sparse principal component analysis, where selecting a small number of participating variables is part of the learning problem.

The authors begin by expressing the sparsity-constrained problem as a mixed integer program. They then use exact penalty techniques to transform it into an equivalent difference-of-convex, or DC, program. The distinction is that their formulation preserves the original problem rather than replacing the count of nonzero entries with an approximation. A customized DC algorithm is used to tackle the resulting formulation.

Computational results on sparse principal component analysis compare the approach favorably with some established methods that approximate the sparsity count. These results support the usefulness of the reformulation in that application. The equivalence concerns the optimization formulations; the abstract does not turn the computational comparison into a claim that every run finds a globally best sparse solution.
icml-2010-a-dc-programming-approach-for-.tldr: An exact DC reformulation offers an alternative to approximating sparsity in eigenvalue problems, with favorable sparse PCA results.

paragraphs: Learning a low-rank matrix means estimating a matrix whose structure can be represented through smaller factors. This paper introduces an augmented Lagrangian algorithm that retains such a compact representation during learning. It does so without requiring the matrix rank to be specified beforehand, combining a flexible representation with an efficient optimization procedure.

The authors report superlinear convergence, describing how rapidly the algorithm approaches its solution. They also show that the framework extends to learning several matrices and to general spectral regularization, which controls properties associated with a matrix's spectrum. The contribution therefore includes both a particular solver and a framework that accommodates related matrix-learning objectives.

The empirical examples make the computational claims concrete. The method recovers a 10,000-by-10,000 matrix from 1.2 million observations in about five minutes. In a brain-computer interface problem, it accelerates optimization by two orders of magnitude relative to conventional projected gradient and produces more reliable solutions. These are reported outcomes for the studied problems, illustrating the practical value of combining compact storage with fast optimization.
icml-2010-a-fast-augmented-lagrangian-al.tldr: A fast low-rank matrix-learning algorithm maintains compact factors without a preset rank and shows substantial computational gains.

paragraphs: Co-training is a semi-supervised learning approach that uses two views of the data and belongs to a broader family of methods organized around disagreement. This paper revisits its theoretical foundations by describing the learning process as a combined form of label propagation across those two views.

That interpretation matters because label propagation also provides a natural language for graph-based semi-supervised learning. The analysis therefore creates a possible route toward treating graph-based and disagreement-based methods within one framework. Instead of viewing them only as separate algorithm families, it asks how the movement of label information across views explains the co-training process.

Within its analysis, the paper provides a condition that is both sufficient and necessary for co-training to succeed. It also relates this result to earlier theoretical work and draws implications for combining weight matrices and splitting data into views. The contribution is a sharper account of when co-training works and how its components relate, rather than an empirical claim of improved accuracy for a new implementation.
icml-2010-a-new-analysis-of-co-training-.tldr: Viewing co-training as label propagation across two views yields a necessary-and-sufficient success condition within the paper's analysis.

paragraphs: Graph Laplacians provide mathematical operators built from connections between data points. Understanding their limiting behavior helps explain what a graph construction represents as its neighborhoods shrink. Earlier analyses commonly required smooth kernel functions, leaving some useful graph constructions outside their scope.

This paper removes that smoothness requirement and extends the analysis to constructions including nearest-neighbor graphs. It also introduces a framework that does not require a kernel description at all. That broader framework handles graph constructions with shrinking neighborhoods and is applied to locally linear embedding, connecting the theoretical analysis to another method for representing data geometry.

The results also address graph design. Starting with a desired limiting operator, the authors describe how an appropriate construction can achieve properties such as sparsity and convergence of the spectrum. This makes the theory relevant to choosing graphs, as well as understanding graphs already chosen. The contribution broadens the available analysis without claiming that every graph construction automatically has these desirable properties.
icml-2010-an-analysis-of-the-convergence.tldr: A broader convergence analysis covers graph Laplacians without smooth kernels and helps connect graph design to desired limiting properties.

paragraphs: Q-learning has a convergence guarantee in single-agent settings with sufficient exploration, but standard analysis becomes inadequate when several agents learn together. This paper studies an idealized version of that interaction in repeated games with two players and two actions, allowing the players' interests to differ.

The authors use dynamical systems methods to analyze epsilon-greedy exploration, whose action-selection behavior introduces discontinuities. They introduce subclasses of these games and provide a complete catalog of convergence behavior for the algorithm in the studied setting. This supplies a value-based counterpart to earlier analyses of gradient-based policy search and highlights differences between the approaches.

One finding concerns two subclasses of games resembling the Prisoner's Dilemma. For some initial conditions, epsilon-greedy Q-learning produces payoffs higher than those at a Nash equilibrium. The qualification about starting conditions is central: the result identifies particular dynamics that can achieve such outcomes. The paper's catalog concerns the specified game setting and idealized learning dynamics, rather than unrestricted multiagent learning.
icml-2010-classes-of-multiagent-q-learni.tldr: An idealized analysis classifies epsilon-greedy Q-learning dynamics in two-player, two-action games and identifies conditional higher-than-Nash outcomes.

paragraphs: This paper studies approximate policy evaluation: estimating how a policy performs in a Markov decision process. Its setting is off-policy learning, where the observations used for evaluation need not come from the policy being evaluated. The specific algorithm is simulation-based least-squares temporal difference learning, LSTD(lambda), for finite state and action spaces.

For a discounted cost objective, the authors establish that off-policy LSTD(lambda) converges almost surely under conditions they describe as mild and minimal. Almost-sure convergence is a probabilistic guarantee about the limiting behavior of the learning process. It strengthens the theoretical basis for using simulated observations to evaluate a policy under the stated setting and conditions.

The analysis also examines convergence and boundedness of intermediate quantities produced by the algorithm. Those properties motivate a suggested modification to its practical implementation, connecting the mathematical results to how the procedure is run. The proofs draw on theories of both finite-state Markov chains and Markov chains on topological spaces, enabling the authors to analyze more than the final estimate alone.
icml-2010-convergence-of-least-squares-t.tldr: Off-policy LSTD(lambda) is shown to converge almost surely under mild conditions for finite MDPs with discounted costs.

paragraphs: Deep belief networks can model high-dimensional visual data, yet ordinary implementations can struggle when images contain occlusion or random noise. This paper explores two ways to improve their robustness. Both concern how the network handles visual information when the input differs from what it encountered during training.

The first strategy changes the network's connections: a sparsely connected first layer is shown to improve robustness to variations absent from the training set. The second strategy introduces probabilistic denoising. It selects a subset of hidden-layer nodes to unclamp, allowing those internal quantities to be reconsidered during denoising instead of keeping them fixed.

The denoising method applies beyond deep belief networks to feed-forward classifiers with localized first-layer connections. That architectural requirement is part of the stated scope of the method. Across various sources of noise, recognition after denoising is significantly better than with standard deep belief network implementations. Together, the findings show how first-layer structure and selective adjustment of hidden representations can improve recognition under corrupted inputs.
icml-2010-deep-networks-for-robust-visua.tldr: Sparse first-layer connections and probabilistic hidden-node denoising improve visual recognition robustness in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Console logs contain information about system behavior, but large services mix enormous numbers of messages from independently developed components. This makes the logs difficult for operators to use when detecting runtime problems. The paper proposes a general methodology for turning that mixed text into information suitable for automated analysis.

The method combines program analysis with information retrieval to convert log messages into numerical features that capture sequences of system events. Machine learning then analyzes those features to detect operational problems. The transformation is a central contribution: it connects software-generated text to a structured representation of behavior that a learning method can examine.

The authors also address how an operator can interpret the result. They distill the analysis into a one-page decision tree showing critical messages associated with detected problems. This links automated detection back to recognizable evidence in the logs. Finally, the methodology is extended to online detection, where event sequences arrive continuously as streams, allowing the same general approach to address ongoing system activity.
icml-2010-detecting-large-scale-system-p.tldr: The paper turns console logs into event-sequence features for automated problem detection and concise operator-facing explanations.

paragraphs: Apprenticeship learning lets a reinforcement-learning agent learn with help from a teacher. In this paper, the teacher supplies policy traces containing observations of transitions and rewards. The authors develop a generalized protocol for using that information across different classes of possible models, rather than centering the protocol on one particular domain.

The theoretical contribution identifies sufficient properties of the underlying models for efficient apprenticeship learning. The authors connect these properties to two established notions of learnability, KWIK and Mistake Bound. These connections provide a way to build on existing learning theory when deciding whether a model class supports an efficient teacher-assisted learning procedure.

The paper then constructs efficient algorithms in several domains, including two kinds of relational Markov decision processes. It also implements the approach in a software agent and a robot agent, both of which learn effectively from a human teacher. The resulting contribution spans a general protocol, sufficient theoretical conditions, and concrete instantiations showing how the framework can support learning from human demonstrations.
icml-2010-generalizing-apprenticeship-le.tldr: A generalized apprenticeship-learning protocol links sufficient efficiency conditions to established learnability classes and supports software and robot learners.

paragraphs: Local Coordinate Coding uses the geometric structure of data to support high-dimensional nonlinear learning. Its representation relies on anchor points, providing a way to describe data through local coordinates. This paper extends that representation with local tangent directions, adding information about how the data's underlying shape behaves near those anchors.

The tangent directions supply correction terms that improve the approximation of nonlinear functions when the underlying data manifold is locally flat. This geometric condition explains when the added terms have the stated benefit. By representing more of the local structure around each anchor, the method significantly reduces the number of anchor points required by the original approach.

The reduced anchor requirement matters both computationally and predictively: the paper reports lower computational cost and improved prediction performance. Experiments on some image classification tasks show greater effectiveness than the original Local Coordinate Coding method. The contribution is thus a specific refinement of a geometry-aware representation, connecting richer local information to a smaller representation and better results in the studied applications.
icml-2010-improved-local-coordinate-codi.tldr: Adding local tangent directions improves Local Coordinate Coding under local flatness and reduces anchor requirements with better reported classification results.

paragraphs: Side information can guide learning through constraints on pairs of examples. However, such constraints may be extracted from imperfect sources, such as links between cited papers, and can therefore be inaccurate. This paper addresses the mismatch between that noisy evidence and learning methods that assume the supplied pairwise constraints are correct.

The authors generalize the maximum entropy model and use it to build a framework for learning from noisy side information. The modeling change makes imperfect pairwise guidance an explicit part of the learning problem. This matters because the usefulness of supplementary relationships depends on how the learner handles errors in those relationships.

The theoretical analysis shows that, under an assumption, a classification model learned from noisy side information can be very close to one learned from perfect side information. The result is conditional and expresses a possibility of robustness under that assumption. Extensive empirical studies support the framework's effectiveness. Together, the theory and experiments establish a case for learning from imperfect relational guidance without requiring that guidance to be error-free.
icml-2010-learning-from-noisy-side-infor.tldr: A generalized maximum entropy framework learns from noisy pairwise constraints, with conditional theoretical support and positive empirical results.

paragraphs: A support vector machine can be easier to use when its prediction depends on only a small subset of input features. This paper tackles feature selection through an explicit sparsity objective. It introduces a binary control variable for each feature, turning the sparse SVM problem into a mixed integer optimization problem.

The authors solve a convex relaxation of that formulation using a cutting-plane algorithm combined with multiple kernel learning. This creates a tractable route to handling feature-selection decisions without directly solving the mixed integer problem. They also provide a global convergence proof for their method; the optimization target remains the stated convex relaxation.

Experiments on one synthetic dataset and ten real-world datasets show better or competitive results relative to existing SVM-based feature-selection methods in both sparsity and generalization. The method also handles large-scale, extremely high-dimensional problems effectively in the reported evaluation. These findings matter because selecting fewer features is useful only if the resulting model also predicts well and the selection procedure remains computationally manageable.
icml-2010-learning-sparse-svm-for-featur.tldr: A cutting-plane and multiple-kernel-learning method solves a convex relaxation of sparse SVM feature selection with competitive empirical results.

paragraphs: This paper addresses control in large Markov decision processes using linear approximations to value functions. It introduces Least-Squares Lambda Policy Iteration, extending least-squares policy iteration through a parameterized approach that generalizes value iteration and policy iteration. The motivation is to bring the flexibility of the lambda parameter into sample-efficient least-squares learning.

The method is designed to work without knowing the process model and without generating a fresh set of samples at every iteration. This makes sample reuse part of the approach, alongside the adjustable policy-iteration procedure. The authors also provide a performance bound supporting the algorithm's theoretical soundness.

Experiments on a simple chain problem and Tetris show that lambda controls a bias-variance trade-off. In practical terms, the parameter changes the balance between systematic approximation error and variability in learning from samples. Adjusting this balance may improve convergence and the performance of the resulting policy. The reported finding is a potential benefit of the parameter, rather than a guarantee that every choice of lambda improves control.
icml-2010-least-squares-policy-iteration.tldr: Least-Squares Lambda Policy Iteration reuses samples while exposing a bias-variance trade-off that may improve convergence and policy performance.

paragraphs: Kernel-based online learners can accumulate more support vectors as training continues, allowing their models to grow without bound. This paper develops budgeted versions of multiclass Pegasos that cap the number of support vectors. For a fixed budget, the algorithms have constant space and time complexity per update.

Enforcing that cap can change the model and reduce its quality. The authors treat this budget-maintenance effect as an error in the gradient used for learning. Their analysis connects the gap from the optimal solution directly to the average model degradation introduced by maintenance. This gives a theoretical reason to focus on how the budget is enforced, rather than considering only its size.

The paper studies greedy maintenance methods that remove, project, or merge support vectors to reduce that degradation. Empirically, the resulting algorithms achieve accuracy comparable to unrestricted multiclass kernelized Pegasos while being highly computationally efficient. The contribution combines bounded resource use with an account of the optimization cost of maintaining that bound.
icml-2010-multi-class-pegasos-on-a-budge.tldr: Budgeted multiclass Pegasos bounds model growth and links its optimization gap to the degradation caused by maintaining the budget.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning objectives compare the probability of the correct label with probabilities assigned to alternatives. Familiar examples concentrate on nearby alternatives. This paper investigates a broader family of objectives that can compare the correct label against an arbitrary set of other configurations, expanding which comparisons can guide learning.

The authors prove that a large class of these objectives is consistent with maximum likelihood even with finite data. Their proof suggests that contrastive objectives impose soft constraints on probability ratios between pairs of configurations. This interpretation explains the objectives through the relationships they encourage between predictions, and generalizes an earlier asymptotic consistency result for pseudo-likelihood.

Using that insight, the paper introduces Contrastive Constraint Generation. This iterative algorithm learns a log-linear model using only maximum a posteriori inference, which identifies the most probable configuration. On a scene classification task, it significantly outperforms pseudo-likelihood, contrastive divergence, and an established margin-based method. The results connect the broader theoretical view of contrastive objectives to a concrete learning algorithm with favorable task-specific evidence.
icml-2010-non-local-contrastive-objectiv.tldr: A probability-ratio interpretation of contrastive objectives motivates an algorithm that learns log-linear models using only MAP inference.

paragraphs: Cost-sensitive classification accounts for differences in the consequences of possible predictions. This paper converts that problem into one-sided regression. The transformation stores cost information in regression targets and uses a one-sided loss to express the goal of choosing the prediction with the lowest cost.

The reduction comes with a theoretical guarantee connecting errors in the regression problem to errors in the classification problem. It is general enough to turn any one-sided regression method into a cost-sensitive classifier. This matters because it provides a supported route for adapting regression machinery to classification decisions governed by unequal costs.

The authors instantiate the reduction with an SVM variant designed for one-sided regression. The resulting classifier can be understood as a theoretically justified extension of one-versus-all SVM classification. Experiments show better cost-sensitive classification performance than traditional one-versus-all SVM and many existing SVM-based cost-sensitive algorithms. The contribution therefore includes both a general reduction and an experimentally evaluated implementation of that reduction.
icml-2010-one-sided-support-vector-regre.tldr: A theoretically supported reduction turns one-sided regression into cost-sensitive classification and yields an effective SVM-based classifier.

paragraphs: Group lasso selects important explanatory factors in groups, making it useful when features have a meaningful grouped structure. This paper develops an online learning algorithm to address the efficiency and scalability problems of traditional batch approaches. The algorithm updates its weights incrementally through a closed-form calculation based on the average of earlier subgradients.

The reported worst-case time complexity and memory cost are both linear in the number of dimensions. This gives a concrete computational basis for the scalability claim. The closed-form update is central because it supplies a direct calculation for each iteration within the online procedure.

The authors extend the system to sparse group lasso variants that encourage sparsity both across groups and among individual features. They also show applicability to overlapping groups and graph lasso, broadening the range of structures the framework can handle. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the algorithm's merits. The paper thus combines an efficient update mechanism with extensions that support more detailed forms of structured feature selection.
icml-2010-online-learning-for-group-lass.tldr: An online group-lasso algorithm uses closed-form updates with linear time and memory costs and extends to several structured sparsity models.

paragraphs: This paper studies a learning setting in which the observations stay fixed while new candidate features arrive one at a time. The final number of features is unknown, and the learner cannot access all of them at the start. Its task is to maintain the best feature set found so far as the stream develops.

The authors introduce a framework based on feature relevance and an algorithm called Online Streaming Feature Selection, or OSFS. It selects strongly relevant features while avoiding redundancy, addressing both whether a feature is useful and whether its information is already represented. A second algorithm, Fast-OSFS, is designed to improve selection efficiency further.

Experiments across various datasets show that the proposed algorithms produce more compact feature sets and better accuracy than existing streaming feature-selection algorithms. The combination matters because a smaller set alone would not establish that the selection preserved useful predictive information. The work directly addresses the practical consequences of receiving features progressively rather than assuming a complete feature space is available before learning begins.
icml-2010-online-streaming-feature-selec.tldr: OSFS and Fast-OSFS select relevant, nonredundant features as features arrive, with improved compactness and accuracy in experiments.

paragraphs: Dimension reduction can reveal useful structure in high-dimensional data, but removing dimensions can also discard predictive information. This paper reframes reduction as a choice about where a model is allowed to search. Learning only in a reduced space restricts the model to a corresponding parameter subspace.

Projection penalties replace that hard restriction with a preference. The model can search the full parameter space, while a penalty discourages distance from the subspace suggested by dimension reduction. This preserves access to directions outside the reduced representation while allowing the reduction to guide learning. The authors develop the framework for linear reductions and extend it to kernel-based and other nonlinear methods.

Experiments cover principal component regression and partial least squares for regression, kernel reduction for face recognition, and topic-based representations for text classification. The reported results show that projection penalties use dimension-reduction techniques more effectively and reliably. The central benefit is preserving the full search space while incorporating the structure supplied by a reduced representation.
icml-2010-projection-penalties-dimension.tldr: Projection penalties use reduced representations to guide learning while keeping the full parameter space available.

paragraphs: Hashing supports approximate nearest-neighbor search by giving data points compact codes that are inexpensive to store and compare. However, the paper identifies a weakness in common hash construction methods: random projections or principal directions can produce codes with poor discrimination when very few bits are available.

The proposed method learns projections from the data in sequence. Each new hash function is designed to correct errors made by the preceding one, so the code is built through successive corrective steps. This makes the relationship between hash functions part of the learning process and directly addresses the challenge of extracting useful distinctions from a compact representation.

The method accommodates both unsupervised and semi-supervised learning scenarios. Experiments on two large datasets, containing up to one million points, show significant gains over the state-of-the-art methods considered. These results support the value of sequential correction for compact hashing in the evaluated settings, where storage savings and fast queries must be balanced against the ability to identify useful neighbors.
icml-2010-sequential-projection-learning.tldr: Learning hash projections sequentially to correct earlier errors improves compact-code nearest-neighbor search in large-dataset experiments.

paragraphs: Multiple kernel learning combines kernels by learning their weights alongside an SVM. Common approaches alternate between optimizing kernel weights and updating the SVM variables. The paper focuses on the kernel-weight step, whose dependence on complicated optimization techniques or commercial software can limit efficiency and applicability.

Using a connection between multiple kernel learning and group lasso, the authors derive a closed-form solution for optimizing the kernel weights. The basic equivalence was already known; their contribution is a variant that enables this efficient calculation. It simplifies a key part of the alternating procedure while retaining the connection to a structured regularization problem.

The paper also extends the equivalence to the family of Lp multiple-kernel-learning models for p at least one. This yields a unified algorithmic treatment across those choices of kernel-weight norm. Experiments on multiple datasets show promising performance compared with competitive methods. The work therefore contributes both a simpler weight-update mechanism and a broader formulation that applies across a family of kernel-learning models.
icml-2010-simple-and-efficient-multiple-.tldr: A group-lasso equivalence yields closed-form kernel-weight updates and a unified algorithm for Lp multiple kernel learning.

paragraphs: Sparse Gaussian process methods reduce computation by representing a large dataset through a smaller set of basis points. A common way to learn that representation is to maximize evidence, but the paper notes that this can be expensive and may lead to overfitting. GPLasso instead makes the balance between approximation quality and sparsity explicit.

Its objective combines a measure of difference between the exact and sparse posterior processes with an L1 penalty that encourages sparse parameters. The difference measure is KL divergence, and the resulting optimization objective is convex. This directly ties model simplicity to how closely the sparse process approximates the full posterior.

The authors further reduce optimization cost using low-rank matrix approximations, including incomplete Cholesky factorization as an example. Experiments compare GPLasso with several sparse Gaussian process methods and direct low-rank approximation methods. The reported result is an improved balance between predictive accuracy and computational cost. The contribution centers on managing that trade-off through an explicit objective together with computationally cheaper matrix operations.
icml-2010-sparse-gaussian-process-regres.tldr: GPLasso balances Gaussian process approximation quality and sparsity through a convex penalized objective, with improved empirical accuracy-cost trade-offs.

paragraphs: Mixed-membership models describe each data point using several components in different proportions. The paper identifies a coupling in the hierarchical Dirichlet process: whether a component appears is positively related to its proportion within a data point. For topic modeling, that can be undesirable when a topic is rare across documents but dominates the few documents where it appears.

The authors introduce the IBP compound Dirichlet process to separate prevalence across data points from proportion within a data point. It combines properties of the hierarchical Dirichlet process and the Indian buffet process. Each data point receives a subset of shared components, called its focus, selected independently of how much those selected components contribute.

The paper applies this prior to text through a focused topic model and reports superior performance over an HDP-based topic model. The modeling contribution is the separation of two questions: which topics belong in a document and how strongly each contributes. That separation accommodates the stated rare-but-dominant topic pattern without imposing the original coupling.
icml-2010-the-ibp-compound-dirichlet-pro.tldr: The IBP compound Dirichlet process separates component occurrence from contribution, enabling a focused topic model with improved reported performance.

paragraphs: This paper develops a probabilistic clustering model for objects represented by pairwise dissimilarities. The authors advocate working directly with that matrix even when a vector representation exists. Their motivation is to avoid unnecessary bias and variance that can arise from first embedding the objects into another representation.

The proposed Translation-invariant Wishart-Dirichlet process uses a Dirichlet process prior, so the number of clusters does not have to be fixed in advance. The model is also invariant to permutation, scale, and translation. These properties define how its clustering formulation responds to changes in ordering and representation, making them part of the model's design rather than additional preprocessing choices.

The authors present an efficient Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling algorithm for inference. Experiments show several advantages over competing approaches, supporting the proposed combination of direct dissimilarity modeling and flexible cluster counts. The stated findings make a case for this probabilistic treatment of distance data; the preference for avoiding embeddings is presented as the authors' modeling argument.
icml-2010-the-translation-invariant-wish.tldr: The TIWD process clusters dissimilarity data directly, with no fixed cluster count and permutation, scale, and translation invariance.

paragraphs: The paper studies the Cheeger cut problem on a weighted graph, where the goal is to find a useful partition of connected objects. Its first contribution is a continuous relaxation: the discrete partitioning problem is expressed through an optimization problem with continuous variables, opening the door to a different set of computational methods.

The authors prove that this relaxation is equivalent to the original problem. That is a stronger statement than simply presenting a continuous surrogate that resembles the graph-cut objective. The equivalence establishes that the relaxed formulation retains the underlying optimization problem, making its mathematical structure directly relevant to finding cuts.

The algorithm is motivated by similarities between the relaxed objective and energies studied in image processing. This connection supplies a practical route from the formulation to a procedure for finding good cuts. Experiments demonstrate efficient discovery of high-quality cuts. The theoretical equivalence and the empirical algorithm results play distinct roles: one validates the formulation, while the other supports the usefulness of the proposed computation.
icml-2010-total-variation-cheeger-cuts-a.tldr: An equivalent continuous formulation of Cheeger cuts motivates an image-processing-inspired algorithm that efficiently finds high-quality cuts in experiments.
